verses.1: Al-Mizan explains iqtarab as extreme nearness and identifies the Hour as the Resurrection. It reads the moon’s splitting as its separation into two parts: a miracle God performed through the Prophet in Mecca before the Emigration, when the idolaters demanded it. Abundant narrations and the traditionists and Qurʾanic commentators support this reading; only al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭāʾ, and al-Balkhī take the past tense as a certain future splitting at the Hour. The commentary rejects that view because the response in (54:2), calling the sign ‘an incessant magic,’ belongs to obstinate idolaters confronted with a miracle, not to the Resurrection when realities are manifest. It likewise rejects an allusion to a scientific separation of moon, earth, and sun: even if that account were true, it neither fits the idolaters’ response nor describes inshiqāq, the moon itself splitting rather than separating from something else. Readings of the phrase as moonrise dispelling darkness or as a metaphor for truth’s manifestation are also rejected. The miracle both establishes the Prophet’s veracity and subtly signals that the Hour’s approach entails it.
verses.2: Al-Mizan takes siḥr mustamirr to mean an incessant magic: one supposed trick following another without ceasing, because mustamirr derives from istimrār, continuous persistence. Since āya is indefinite, the deniers’ response applies generally to every sign they witness. It records readings of mustamirr as permanent, fleeting, repugnant, or offensive, but judges them remote from its apparent meaning.
verses.3: Al-Mizan understands the denial as denial of the Prophet and the signs he brought. Every matter will reach the point at which it settles and its truth or falsity becomes known; then the truthfulness of the Prophet and his cause will be clear. It rejects restricting their denial to the moon’s splitting, because the clause about every matter having a setting does not fit that reading.
verses.4: Al-Mizan says that the reports containing admonishment may mean the accounts of nations destroyed by God or prophecies of Resurrection; the following sequence of Resurrection reports and destroyed peoples indicates both together. It defines ḥikma bāligha as true, beneficial, complete wisdom, perfect both in itself and in effect. The Qurʾan, or the message to which they are called, is such wisdom, but because they deny and follow desire, neither warners nor warnings avail them.

verses.6: Al-Mizan grounds the command fa tawalla ʿanhum in the deniers’ rejection of prophethood and pursuit of desire: repeated warning and admonition will not affect them, so the Prophet is told to turn away. It treats ‘the day when the Caller calls to a dire thing’ as a fresh answer to the implied question of what will become of them, not as a continuation of that command. The phrase may qualify their emergence from the graves, or elliptically command mention of that day; in either case it concerns the judgment and recompense facing people who resemble earlier deniers. The caller is left unnamed here, although elsewhere the call is ascribed to God. Their Resurrection scene deliberately parallels their present response to divine signs: unlike their turning away and calling them magic, they emerge fearful and humbled from their graves, mingling like scattered locusts and scrambling toward the summoner. The faithless then acknowledge it as a hard day.

verses.9: Al-Mizan reads the two uses of takdhīb as a general statement that Noah’s people denied and an explanation that they denied Noah, though it allows the sound reading that denial of Noah meant denial of all messengers, whose message is one. It rejects as far-fetched readings that make the first denial continuous across generations or merely intended rather than performed. Calling Noah ‘Our servant’ both honors him and makes their repudiation of him tantamount to repudiating God, since a servant possesses nothing independently of his master. Their charge that he was mad and possessed says that a jinn caused his speech, rather than that it was revelation. The commentary regards more fitting than the alternative reading in which wa-zdujir means that they restrained Noah through threats and persecution.
verses.10: Al-Mizan explains Noah’s appeal for intiṣār as a call for divine retribution after his people had forcibly suppressed him, not defeated his arguments. The verse gives only a summary of his supplication; its fuller form and his arguments with his people occur in Sūrah Hūd and elsewhere.
verses.11: Al-Mizan reads the opened gates of heaven as a metaphor for violent, uninterrupted rain, as if water held behind gates had been released. It explains fajjarnā al-arḍ as splitting the earth so that underground springs flow abundantly. The heavenly and earthly waters met according to God’s preordained plan, neither exceeding it nor arriving earlier or later; ‘water’ is singular as the name of the species embracing both. Their ordained purpose was the Flood.

verses.13: Al-Mizan identifies the vessel as Noah’s ark, built from wooden alwāḥ fastened by dusur, and considers competing meanings less suitable to the context. Its sailing ‘in Our sight’ means that it crossed the flood under divine protection, guardianship, and oversight; a suggestion that this means the sight of God’s allies and assigned angels is also reported. The rescue of those aboard recompensed Noah, whom his people had rejected, and illustrates God’s reward for the virtuous.

verses.15: Al-Mizan takes the retained sign to be Noah’s ark, through which Noah and his companions were saved: it calls people to reflect on God’s oneness, the truth of the prophets’ call, and the severity of divine punishment. It therefore infers that the ark remained until the revelation. The commentary reports claims that it was on Mount Jūdī and a transmitted report that early Muslims found wood from it near Mount Ararat, while noting the alternative that ‘it’ means the details of the story.
verses.16: Al-Mizan takes the rhetorical question as a terrifying assertion of the severity of God’s punishment and the truth of His warnings.
verses.17: Al-Mizan says that God makes the Qurʾan easy for people of every social standing, education, and intellectual capacity, each according to their capacity. It may also mean that transcendent realities beyond human comprehension have been sent down as intelligible Arabic speech. Citing al-Rāghib, it notes that dhikr can concern the soul’s retention or recall of knowledge, a thing’s presence in the heart, or verbal mention; here it is remembrance of God through His names, attributes, and acts. The verse is therefore a general summons to remember God, believe, and follow the true religion after the warning’s truth and punishment’s severity have been affirmed. The unconnected opening of the next story makes each destroyed people an independent warning. In the case of ʿĀd, the question about punishment and warnings introduces the coming account and draws attention to its terror, rather than, as before, frightening the audience after the punishment has been described.

verses.19: Al-Mizan describes ṣarṣar as a fiercely gusting wind and yawm naḥs mustamirr as a period continuously disastrous for ʿĀd, with no prospect of relief. ‘Day’ need not mean a literal day, since the Qurʾan elsewhere speaks of ill-fated days and of seven nights and eight days; some commentators also understand naḥs as cold. The wind itself knocked people down, leaving their bodies like uprooted palm trunks.

verses.21:
Al-Mizan treats the repeated warning and invitation to remembrance as already explained, then considers whether times can be inherently good- or ill-fated. Reason can neither establish nor decisively exclude this, because time is uniform and the causes shaping events are not fully known; mere improbability is not impossibility. Revelation calls the period in which ʿĀd were punished ill-fated, but the context confines this to the seven nights and eight days of the unceasing punishment, not to an intrinsic quality of that week recurring through months and years. By contrast, the blessedness of Laylat al-Qadr is connected to spiritual events and grace—such as the resolution of decree and descent of the angels—and to the special merit and reward of worship then.

Al-Mizan says that many reports about ominous weekdays and calendar dates have weak or incomplete chains, though a few may be reliable. In many, a day is deemed ill-fated because an event offensive to religious feeling occurred on it, such as the death of the Prophet, the martyrdom of Imām Ḥusayn, or a punishment; avoiding ordinary enjoyment on such a day can foster piety, while disregarding its religious association can show contempt for religion. Reports that prescribe loyalty to the Imāms, almsgiving, fasting, supplication, and Qurʾanic recitation to repel ill fortune, alongside reports telling people not to blame innocent days for recompense of their own deeds, redirect popular superstition toward God and explain its effect principally through the psyche. The commentary considers it not unlikely that traditions affirming inherent ill fortune were uttered in taqiyya, given the widespread popular belief. It concludes that no evidence establishes an innate natural power in days; traditions apparently asserting one must be read as taqiyya or as baseless.

On heavenly bodies, Al-Mizan likewise finds no rational proof that particular planets or alignments are auspicious or inauspicious. It records ancient accounts that treat them as ensouled agents, unensouled agents, signs accompanying God’s acts, or merely occasions on which God habitually creates events. Reports and remarkable accounts may indicate a partial connection between celestial and terrestrial events, so no categorical judgment is possible. A dependent, intermediate role for planets would not by itself contradict religion; making them independent creators, or independent directors of the cosmic order, would attribute rubūbiyya and maʿbūdiyya to them and be polytheism. Reports ascribed to the Imāms both mention favorable and unfavorable alignments and warn against astrology; Al-Mizan reconciles the prohibition with permissive reports by directing it at belief in an influence independent of God, while other reports say little astrological knowledge is useless and much unattainable. A report that the People of the House possess such knowledge supports only a general connection, and the story of Jupiter teaching it to men appears fabricated.

Al-Mizan finally distinguishes taking a good omen, tafāʾul, which Islam encourages, from taṭayyur, taking a bad omen, which it forbids. Their frequent apparent accuracy is traced to their effect on the believer’s psyche. Qurʾanic prophets answer those who call them an ill omen by locating benefit and harm with God, not with an omen. Traditions therefore tell people to ignore bad omens, trust God, and supplicate; calling superstition polytheism underscores that nothing harms independently of His leave.

verses.23: Al-Mizan allows nudhur to mean Ṣāliḥ’s warnings, the warners in the sense that denying one messenger denies them all because their message is one, or warnings in the plural; the last can bear either of the first two senses. Thamūd add that following a wāḥid would leave them in error and suʿur, which here figuratively means madness rather than its literal blazing fires. Wāḥid may stress that Ṣāliḥ was a lone, powerless man with no followers, unlike the influential figures they were accustomed to obey, or simply that he was one of their own human kind. Their objection excuses rejection of his summons to obey him rather than their profligate grandees.
verses.24: Al-Mizan allows nudhur to mean Ṣāliḥ’s warnings, the warners in the sense that denying one messenger denies them all because their message is one, or warnings in the plural; the last can bear either of the first two senses. Thamūd add that following a wāḥid would leave them in error and suʿur, which here figuratively means madness rather than its literal blazing fires. Wāḥid may stress that Ṣāliḥ was a lone, powerless man with no followers, unlike the influential figures they were accustomed to obey, or simply that he was one of their own human kind. verses.25: Al-Mizan takes Thamūd’s question as a rhetorical denial: they deem it impossible that revelation should be given exclusively to Ṣāliḥ, whom they consider no better than themselves. ‘Cast upon him’ may stress the sudden, unexpected character they attribute to this claim. More fundamentally, they reject revelation’s coming to one human being among them: if it were genuine and possible for a human, they reason, why was everyone not given it? Their charge that he is a self-conceited liar means that he is vainly seeking superiority over them.
verses.26: Al-Mizan identifies these as God’s words to Ṣāliḥ. ‘Tomorrow’ means the eventual outcome, not the next literal day: when punishment comes, Thamūd will know with certainty whether Ṣāliḥ or they were the self-conceited liars.
verses.27: Al-Mizan explains fitna as a test and ordeal. God will send the miraculously demanded she-camel to test Thamūd; Ṣāliḥ is told to observe what they do and remain steadfast against their persecution.
verses.28: Al-Mizan defines shirb as a share of water. Ṣāliḥ must tell his people that water is apportioned between them and the she-camel: each has its appointed turn to drink. A translator’s note explains that the plural pronoun includes both the people and the she-camel through taghlīb, the grammatical preference for one member of an interrelated pair.
verses.29: Al-Mizan identifies ‘their companion’ as the man who undertook the task of hamstringing and killing the she-camel.
verses.30: Al-Mizan explains muḥtaẓir as a maker of an animal pen and hashīm as the dry branches used to build it. Thamūd were reduced by a single Cry to such dry sticks.
verses.31: Al-Mizan explains muḥtaẓir as a maker of an animal pen and hashīm as the dry branches used to build it. Thamūd were reduced by a single Cry to such dry sticks.
verses.32: Al-Mizan says that this recurring declaration of the Qurʾan’s ease for remembrance has already been explained.
verses.33: Al-Mizan says that the statement about Lot’s people denying the warnings has the same explanation as (54:23).
verses.34: Al-Mizan reads ḥāṣib as a powerful wind carrying stones and pebbles, the rain of stones of laminated shale, from which Lot’s family was saved. It notes that indefinite bi saḥarin means at a dawn on some morning, unlike a definite expression for this very morning.
verses.35: Al-Mizan takes niʿmatan as expressing the purpose of Lot’s family’s deliverance: it was a particular divine blessing granted because they were grateful. Salvation is thus the recompense for gratitude.
verses.36: Al-Mizan identifies ‘he’ as Lot, baṭsha as severe punishment, and tamārū as obstinate disputation and persistence in doubt. Lot had warned his people of God’s severe punishment, but they disputed those warnings.
verses.37: Al-Mizan says that Lot’s people demanded he hand over his guests, who were angels, and that God then blinded them. The abrupt direct address—‘Taste My punishment and My warnings!’—expresses God’s wrath and rebuke; nudhur here means the severe punishment of which they had been warned.
verses.38: Al-Mizan explains that indefinite bukratan denotes a future dawn rather than the following day’s specific dawn. The punishment is mustaqirr, abiding: none were spared and it did not cease.
verses.39: Al-Mizan says that the formula commanding them to taste punishment and warnings, and the recurring declaration that the Qurʾan is easy for remembrance, have already been explained.
verses.40: Al-Mizan says that the formula commanding them to taste punishment and warnings, and the recurring declaration that the Qurʾan is easy for remembrance, have already been explained.
verses.41: Al-Mizan explains the lack of a conjunction as making Pharaoh’s clan’s denial the answer to the implicit question raised by the arrival of the warnings: what did they do? They denied every sign, and God consequently seized them with the seizing of the all-mighty, Omnipotent One.
verses.42: Al-Mizan explains the lack of a conjunction as making Pharaoh’s clan’s denial the answer to the implicit question raised by the arrival of the warnings: what did they do? They denied every sign, and God consequently seized them with the seizing of the all-mighty, Omnipotent One.
verses.43: Al-Mizan takes the rhetorical question as addressed to the Prophet’s people, perhaps to both believers and disbelievers because it says ‘your faithless,’ though its primary concern may be the disbelievers among them. Their alleged superiority to the peoples of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd, Lot, and Pharaoh may concern worldly advantages such as wealth and children or civic virtues such as generosity, courage, and care for the weak. Either way, the answer is denial: their faithless are not better than the destroyed nations and will not escape punishment. The second rhetorical question asks whether they possess an immunity in the revealed zubur—divine books sent to prophets—that exempts their disbelief and sin from God’s punishment or judgment.
verses.44: Al-Mizan defines jamīʿ as a group emphasizing unity of decision and action. Muntaṣir may derive from seeking revenge or mutual support, so the disbelievers boast either that their considerable, united numbers will avenge harm or that they will support one another and cannot be driven off.
verses.45: Al-Mizan says that the league in which the disbelievers trust will be defeated, turn its back, and flee. It reads this as a Qurʾanic prophecy of their routing in a war they initiated, fulfilled at Badr.
verses.46: Al-Mizan defines adhā as the gravest inescapable calamity and amarr as more bitter than sweetness. The verse moves from defeat and worldly punishment to the final destination of the disbelievers: the Hour and Final Judgment, to which the preceding account had pointed. That fate exceeds every worldly calamity in disaster and bitterness.
verses.47: Al-Mizan defines suʿur as raging fires and explains why the Hour is more calamitous and bitter: the guilty have strayed from the path to everlasting felicity and Paradise into blazing fire.
verses.48: Al-Mizan makes ‘the day’ qualify the preceding state of error and fires. Saqar is a name of hell, and its ‘touch’ is the heat and torment afflicting them as they are dragged face-down into the Fire and told to taste it.
verses.49:
Al-Mizan defines qadar as the limit, shape, and appointed course that no created thing exceeds or departs from. The verse answers why the guilty meet error and Fire: human beings are created to multiply and form societies, take provision in this transient life for the enduring one, and receive messengers who call them to happiness in both. Those who answer attain happiness, Paradise, and nearness to their Lord; those who reject and persist in sin enter error and hellfire.

Al-Mizan considers the objection that this answer begs the question—explaining God’s decree to punish by His decree—mistaken. Human actions are judged by universal principles abstracted from objective, entified existence and by external causes such as hunger and its satisfaction. God’s actions, however, are identical with that existence; the principles derived from it are posterior to, and patterned on, His acts. No cause outside Him can explain or validate His action, so asking ‘why’ in search of an external cause or prior universal standard is meaningless.

The commentary nevertheless says that Qurʾanic rationales for divine acts take three forms. They may state outcomes or benefits for creatures, which explain the act’s place in causal order rather than a motive benefiting God. They may invoke a divine name or attribute suited to a particular act, explaining a specific aspect through a general one. Or they may explain one specific divine act through another, general act; this ultimately returns to the second form. Here qadar is the general divine act that fixes the limits of all things, and punishment is a specific form of that measurement because rejecting the prophets’ call leads human beings to hellfire. Such explanation is at the level of subsistence, thubūt, rather than demonstration, ithbāt, and so is not begging the question.

Al-Mizan then reads amr as a creative command, amr takwīnī, rather than a legislative command or an ‘affair’: God’s word ‘Be.’ Calling it a single thing means that no repetition is required for its intended result, and comparing it to an eye’s twinkling concerns the immediacy of realization, not a momentary duration. God’s bringing things into being requires no time, space, or movement, since these themselves exist by His command. Thus all created existence, as God’s act, is like a blink even where it appears gradual in objective reality. In the immediate threat, the Hour and renewed creation through Resurrection need only one divine command, completing the point that everything is created with measure.

verses.51: Al-Mizan takes ashyāʿ as people of former nations like the audience in disbelief and denial of prophets. Their destruction confirms that warnings of punishment in this world and at the Hour are not empty claims: such people were destroyed, will meet punishment in the Hereafter, and have their deeds preserved in records for reckoning and requital.
verses.52: Al-Mizan takes zubur to mean records of people’s deeds, not the Guarded Tablet, al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ. In context, ‘big and small’ encompasses major and minor deeds, all of which are recorded.
verses.53: Al-Mizan takes zubur to mean records of people’s deeds, not the Guarded Tablet, al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ. In context, ‘big and small’ encompasses major and minor deeds, all of which are recorded.
verses.54: Al-Mizan describes the Godwary as amid gardens and nahar, understood as magnificent streams, though some take nahar as expansiveness. Their maqʿad is an abode or assembly before the malīk muqtadir, God the omnipotent Sovereign. Ṣidq may be the truthfulness of their untainted belief and action, which makes them ever present, near, blessed, happy, and enduring there; or it may be the truth of God’s promise itself. The latter contrasts their certain, undeceptive reward and nearness with the guilty people’s threatened error and punishment under irrevocable qadar.
